title: The nap
hookLine: rest itself is a mitzvah on Shabbat
tomorrow: the Talmud says read the portion twice, then once more. why?

lines: I WAS JUST RESTING MY EYES.
cards: Saturday, two in the afternoon. Noa comes downstairs and finds her mom, Rachel, asleep on the couch, reading glasses still on, a roll of house plans sliding off her lap. Rachel never naps.
She's an architect; she sketches through dinner and answers clients from the car.

Noa reaches for the plans to roll them up, and Rachel wakes with a jolt, already apologizing: I wasn't sleeping, I was just resting my eyes. As if she'd been caught at something. So which was it, lazy or holy?

teach.b: Exodus calls the Sabbath a sign, because God made heaven and earth in six days, and then, in the King James Version, "on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed." The Hebrew verb is vayinafash.
It shares its letters with nefesh, a word for soul or breath, so some readers hear it this way: on the seventh day, God caught his breath. Sit with how bold that is. The verse puts rest on God.
If the One who made heaven and earth stops to be refreshed, then a person stopping to sleep on Shabbat isn't slacking. It's imitation.

teach.h: SLEEP ON SHABBAT IS A DELIGHT.
teach.b: An old Hebrew saying puts it in three words, shena b'Shabbat ta'anug: sleep on Shabbat is a delight. Some point out that the first letters of the saying spell Shabbat.
But there's a catch, and it's the part to tell a friend tonight. A later law code says a person shouldn't announce, let's sleep now so we can work late tonight.
The nap isn't fuel for Sunday's to-do list.
It's rest for its own sake, the kind that isn't earning anything. Back on the couch, Rachel is still apologizing. She doesn't need to.
She wasn't caught. She was keeping the day.

how: A Shabbat afternoon nap is a well-loved custom among Jews who keep the day, often after the long midday meal; the old saying shena b'Shabbat ta'anug, sleep on Shabbat is a delight, is quoted with a smile.

o: Shabbat rest, taken without guilt, as part of the day
the long sleep that some take on Yom Kippur
a quick rest so you can work late after Shabbat

games.q: the holy nap — tap the pairs.
p: sleep on Shabbat is a delight
don't nap to work late tonight

s: Exodus describes God as resting and being refreshed on the seventh day
napping on Shabbat is a lazy habit the tradition puts up with
an old saying calls sleep on Shabbat a delight, and the verse puts rest on God.
it's ideal to nap on Shabbat so you can work all night after
a later law code says not to frame Shabbat rest as fuel for weekday work.

games.q: your friend works double shifts and says she sleeps on Saturday afternoons "to recharge for Monday." what would the Shabbat view add?
o: the rest is holy in itself, not only fuel for Monday.
she's right: Shabbat rest exists to make the work better.
she should stay awake and use the time to study instead.
games.why: a later law code says not to say, let's sleep so we can work tonight. the rest belongs to the day, not to the to-do list.

practice: Lie down if you can, or lean all the way back in your chair. Let your weight drop into whatever is holding you, the floor, the couch, the seat, and let your hands go loose.
No goal for this rest: it isn't getting you ready for anything.

wordCard.voice: The nap: Shabbat rest taken without guilt, because even God, says Exodus, rested and was refreshed.

orig.note: Hebrew: and was refreshed, from Exodus 31:17; it shares its letters with nefesh, soul or breath.

carryVoice: Something to hold: rest is holy, part of the day itself and not a reward for surviving the week. Sleep well.

sources.q: on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed

sources.ref: Folk saying: shena b'Shabbat ta'anug (sleep on Shabbat is a delight)
Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 290:2 (one should not say, let us sleep so we can work after Shabbat)
